title: What helps children cope with anxiety before an operation
intro: Many children feel afraid before an operation. Fear of the unknown, of pain or of being separated from parents is common. Honest, age-appropriate preparation and calm support from adults can greatly reduce anxiety and help recovery.

sections.heading: Prepare honestly
paragraphs: Explain in simple words what will happen, using truthful language suited to age. Tell the child why the operation is needed, that they will be asleep and will not feel it, and that it will be sore afterwards but pain relief will be given. Avoid false promises. Give information a few days before for younger children and earlier for older ones.

sections.heading: Use play and visits
paragraphs: Books, drawings and play with dolls or toys can show the steps. Many hospitals offer tours, videos, or preparation programmes with child life specialists. Seeing the ward, the equipment and the staff reduces fear. Let the child ask questions and express feelings.

sections.heading: Staying close
paragraphs: Parents are usually allowed to stay with the child before the operation and be present when they fall asleep, and to be there on waking. Parents who stay calm help the child feel safe. Bring a favourite toy or blanket, and music or a tablet for distraction.

sections.heading: Medical support
paragraphs: Sometimes a mild sedative is given before the operation. Anaesthetists use techniques such as a mask with sweet-smelling gas, or numbing cream for needles. Distraction, bubbles, breathing games and virtual reality can help. Tell staff if your child is very fearful so that they can adapt.

sections.heading: Afterwards
paragraphs: Reassure the child, praise bravery, give pain relief and allow time to talk about what happened. Changes in sleep, clinginess or behaviour may occur for a few weeks. If they continue or worsen, ask for help.

examples.title: Preparing at home
examples.text: Imagine your child has an operation next week. You could read a picture book about hospital and role-play with a toy doctor.

examples.title: Choosing distraction
examples.text: Suppose your child fears needles. You might ask for numbing cream and bring a tablet with a favourite film.
